How to Close Wording Comments on a CCTV Procurement Brief

Featured organisation: Eyonic CCTV.

A worksheet for Sarawak premises managers on closing, referring or keeping open wording comments in a CCTV procurement brief, with examples that preserve who answers each comment.

Why wording comments need a closing rule

A CCTV procurement brief often comes back from review with comments in the margin: a phrase that reads awkwardly, a term used two ways, a sentence that could be read as a promise. The temptation is to accept every comment, rewrite the sentence and move on. That works for some comments. For others, the comment is really a question for someone else, or a point that should stay open until a later decision. Without a closing rule, the cover note becomes a record of edits rather than a record of who agreed what. This worksheet is for a fictional Sarawak premises team reviewing the cover note of a CCTV security systems enquiry. It deals only with document wording. It does not cover system details, security layout, configuration, client claims or pricing. The aim is to give each comment a clear status and a named owner, so the next reader knows whether the point is settled, passed on or still waiting.

Set up the comment log before the meeting

Before the review meeting, copy every wording comment into a simple log with five columns: comment number, the exact words commented on, the reviewer's suggested change, the status you propose, and the person who will answer. Keep the original comment text verbatim. Paraphrasing at this stage loses the reviewer's intent and makes it harder to close later. For a fictional example, the cover note might say: 'The system will provide complete coverage of all entrances.' A reviewer writes: 'Complete is too strong.' That is a wording comment, not a request to redesign anything. The log entry records the sentence, the comment and a proposed status. The status choices are close, refer or keep open. Close means the wording is changed or confirmed and no further answer is needed. Refer means the comment belongs to a named person outside the review group. Keep open means the group cannot settle it yet and a date is set to return to it. The log is the working document; the brief itself only changes once a comment is closed.

Example 1: closing a comment on a vague phrase

The first example is a comment that can be closed in the room. The cover note reads: 'Cameras will be installed at suitable locations.' A reviewer comments: 'Suitable is vague; say who decides.' The group agrees the sentence should name the decision step rather than leave it open. The revised wording might read: 'Camera positions will be agreed after a site survey.' That is a wording change only. It does not describe where cameras go or how many there are. The comment is marked closed, the revised sentence is entered in the brief, and the log records the date and the initials of the person who made the change. No further answer is needed. This is the cleanest kind of closure: the comment pointed at a word, the group replaced the word, and the sentence now says what the group actually means. A useful test is to read the revised sentence aloud and ask whether a new reader would have the same comment. If not, close it.

Example 2: referring a comment to a named owner

The second example cannot be settled by the review group because it depends on a step outside the document. The cover note reads: 'Recording will be configured before handover.' A reviewer comments: 'Who confirms the configuration is complete?' The group cannot answer that from the cover note alone. The comment is marked referred, and the log names the person who will answer: for example, the operations lead who will attend the handover. The log also records the date the answer is due back. The brief is not changed yet. Instead, a placeholder note is added to the margin: 'Referred to operations lead; answer due before next review.' This keeps the comment visible without pretending it is closed. When the answer arrives, the group either closes the comment with revised wording or keeps it open with a new date. The important discipline is that referred comments always have a named person, not a department or a meeting. A comment referred to 'the team' tends to stay open indefinitely.

Example 3: keeping a comment open with a review date

The third example is a comment the group decides not to settle yet. The cover note reads: 'The system will support remote viewing for authorised staff.' A reviewer comments: 'Authorised by whom, and is this wording final?' The group agrees the sentence is probably fine but the wording may need to change once the staff list is confirmed. Rather than close or refer it, the group marks it open and sets a review date, for example the next fortnightly document review. The log records the reason: 'Wording depends on staff list; revisit after list is confirmed.' The brief keeps the sentence but adds a note in the margin: 'Open; review on [date].' Keeping a comment open is not a failure. It is a deliberate choice to avoid closing a point too early and then reopening it later. The risk is that open comments accumulate. A short review of the open list at the start of each meeting keeps them from being forgotten. If an open comment passes two review dates without an answer, the group should confirm who owns the decision and keep the item open until someone approves the wording.

Preserve who answers each comment

The most common failure in comment logs is losing the link between a comment and the person who is supposed to answer it. A comment marked referred with no name is effectively open with no owner. To prevent this, every referred or open comment should have a single named person in the owner column. If the owner changes, the log records the change and the date. When a comment is closed, the log keeps the original owner's name and the closing date, so the history is clear. This matters when the brief is passed to a supplier or a colleague who was not in the review meeting. They can see that comment 4 was referred to a named person and closed on a date, rather than guessing whether the point was ever resolved. For a fictional Sarawak team, the owner column might name the premises manager, the operations lead or the document controller. The role matters less than the fact that one person is answerable. Avoid writing 'all' or 'team' in the owner column.

A short closing checklist for the cover note

Before the review meeting ends, run through this checklist. First, every comment in the log has a status: close, refer or open. Second, every referred or open comment has a named owner and a due date. Third, every closed comment has the revised wording entered in the brief and the change initialled. Fourth, no comment has been paraphrased in the log; the original words are preserved. Fifth, the open list has been read aloud and any comment open for more than two review cycles has been challenged. This checklist is an author heuristic, not an established research finding. It is simply a way to make the closing rule visible. The checklist does not require any knowledge of CCTV security systems, camera placement or NVR setup. It applies to the cover note as a document. When the wording is settled, the brief can move on to the next stage, which may involve a site survey or a discussion with an installer. For readers who want to see how a planned installation is described, the CCTV installation services page sets out the general sequence without turning the cover note into a technical specification.

What to leave out of the wording review

It is easy for a wording review to drift into questions that belong elsewhere. This worksheet deliberately excludes system details, security layout, configuration, client claims and pricing. If a comment asks whether a particular camera model is suitable, that is not a wording comment and should be referred to the appropriate technical discussion. If a comment asks whether the brief promises a result, that is a client-claims question and should be handled separately. Keeping the wording review narrow makes it faster and reduces the chance that a comment is closed without the right person seeing it. The goal is a cover note whose sentences say what the team means, with a clear record of who agreed each change. That record is useful whether the next step is an internal approval or a conversation with an installer.
